description: When a Moon mission’s launch slips, one crater rim can kill the landing site. We’re building the tool that tells planners instantly whether a site still gets sunlight and Earth contact, and where to land instead if it doesn’t.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app for choosing where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. Pick any site and date, and it tells you GO, MARGINAL or NO-GO. It bases that on how much sunlight the solar panels will get, whether the crew can stay in contact with Earth, how steep and rough the ground is, how cold it gets, and space-weather risk.

Everything is calculated from real NASA data. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL ephemerides, the terrain and horizons from LOLA laser altimetry, and the maps of always-dark craters from Goddard’s PGDA. Temperatures are measured by Diviner, and solar-storm alerts come from DONKI. Users explore a 3D globe, replay the Sun’s and Earth’s paths over the mission, and scan a 365-day launch calendar. The app also suggests nearby sites with better windows and steers landers away from the always-dark craters.

Hadfield, a voice assistant, finds the best spot for any date. If a crew reports a fuel leak or power loss, it decides whether to divert and where. Standard, Learn and Expert modes serve the public, students and mission planners.

As Artemis returns humans to the Moon, landing-site choices decide whether a mission has power, communications and safety.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps people decide where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. Choose a site (a past landing, an Artemis III candidate region, or any spot on the globe) and a launch date. The app then checks the whole mission window and gives a GO, MARGINAL or NO-GO verdict with plain reasons. It checks:

  • Sunlight: how much of the mission the Sun is above the local horizon (solar power), and the longest stretch of darkness.
  • Earth contact: how often Earth is above the antenna limit (direct communication).
  • Terrain: slope and roughness at the pad, from laser-altimeter maps.
  • Temperature: the surface temperature range measured from orbit, plus an estimate for the mission dates.
  • Permanently shadowed regions (PSRs): craters that never see sunlight. The app outlines them, keeps a 500 m safety buffer, and moves any pad placed inside one to the nearest safe spot.
  • Space weather: solar particle events reported for the mission window.

How it works

  • The Python backend computes Sun and Earth positions with JPL’s DE421 ephemeris (using Skyfield). It then compares them with the real terrain horizon around each site, built from NASA LOLA elevation maps.
  • Our calculated Sun positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.0004°, and the app shows this check in a built-in NASA Validation panel.
  • A two-stage search scans the whole south pole for flat, sunlit pads outside permanently shadowed regions. It then evaluates the best candidates in detail.
  • The web app shows a 3D Moon globe with real polar terrain. It draws the Sun’s and Earth’s paths across the mission, includes a mission timeline you can scrub through, and has a 365-day launch calendar that colour-codes every possible launch day.

Key features

  • Rapid scenario comparison: nearby alternative sites appear beside the calendar, with their GO-day counts and best launch windows.
  • Hadfield, the AI mission assistant: works by voice or text. Ask “what’s the best landing spot on January 10?” and it searches the pole, moves the lander there, sets the date and opens the calendar on the best day. Report an anomaly, such as a fuel leak, power loss or comms failure, and it tightens the limits that problem affects. It then judges whether the current pad still works and, if not, relocates to a reachable pad that does.
    • Standard for quick decisions.
    • Learn for students, with plain-language explanations, a glossary and everyday comparisons.
    • Expert for mission planners, with solar-power and temperature curves, battery sizing for the longest night, slope pass/fail against an adjustable limit, and ice/hydrogen indicators.
  • Earth vs Moon comparison: a side-by-side view of terrain, atmosphere, gravity, temperature and radiation.
  • Works on phones, tablets and desktops. Any scenario can be shared as a link.

Benefits and intended impact

As Artemis returns crews to the Moon, the south pole’s extreme lighting makes the choice of site and date decisive. A pad a few kilometres away, or a launch a few days later, can mean the difference between continuous power and contact with Earth, and long freezing nights cut off from Earth. Our tool turns large NASA datasets into answers in seconds.

  • Mission planners can compare scenarios quickly and plan contingencies.
  • Students and the public can see why a site works, not just whether it does.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy, SciPy and Rasterio.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Zustand and Tailwind CSS. Hadfield’s voice uses the browser’s built-in speech recognition and speech synthesis.
  • AI: Hadfield runs on a free Google Gemma 4 model via OpenRouter. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant during development.
  • Hosting: Vercel for the website; Cloudflare Tunnel to connect the backend.
  • Hardware: standard laptops only.

NASA data used: DE421 / NAIF SPICE kernels, JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA terrain (240 m polar, global, and 5 m site maps), PGDA Sun visibility, Earth visibility and permanently-shadowed-region maps, LRO Diviner temperatures, DONKI space weather, Moon Trek, and the SVS CGI Moon Kit.

What makes it creative

  • It treats landing as a question of place and time together. The calendar and nearby-site comparison show that waiting a few days or moving a few kilometres can turn NO-GO into GO.
  • It pairs real ephemeris and terrain physics with a conversational AI that acts. Hadfield doesn’t only answer; it moves the lander, changes the date and opens the right panels, and every action can be undone with one click.
  • Anomaly-aware relocation: each problem tightens only the limits it affects. A damaged landing leg needs a nearly level pad, while a battery fault caps how long the night can be.
  • One tool serves three audiences through its modes, from a curious student to a flight planner.

Factors we considered

  • Data honesty: every number is labelled measured, est., illustrative or typical, so model results are never mistaken for observations. The hydrogen and ice values are clearly marked illustrative.
  • Crew safety: a 500 m buffer around permanently shadowed regions; slope and roughness limits; and the rule that once landed, the lander cannot relocate.
  • Accuracy: the app checks its own maths against JPL Horizons.
  • Accessibility: voice input and output, plain-language Learn mode, keyboard support, and layouts for phones and tablets.
  • Speed: precomputed polar maps and caching keep whole-pole searches to about a second.
  • Security: API keys stay on the server and are never sent to the browser.
  • Limits we state openly: pass/fail thresholds are our engineering choices, not NASA requirements, and the tool is a planning aid, not flight-certified.
